vignette: Asher had always been proud of his ability to stay calm under pressure. As an architect, he was used to managing complex projects and tight deadlines. But everything changed on that fateful day three years ago when he witnessed a violent altercation between two men in the parking garage near his office building. Asher had been walking back from lunch when he stumbled upon the scene - one man pinned against a car, the other looming over him with a raised fist. The sounds and smells of that moment were forever seared into Asher's memory: the crunch of metal, the scent of gasoline, and the stench of sweat. He remembered trying to step in, but his legs felt like lead, unable to move as the attacker turned towards him. The next thing he knew, he was running back to the safety of his office building, his heart racing. In the days that followed, Asher began to notice changes in himself. He couldn't shake off the feeling of being constantly on edge - scanning for exits whenever he entered a room, positioning himself with his back against a wall so he could see everything happening around him. The smell of gasoline would trigger a wave of nausea, transporting him back to that moment in the parking garage. Asher struggled to put into words what had happened. When he tried to explain it to his wife or friends, he felt like he was reliving the event all over again. His memories were jumbled and out of sequence - he couldn't seem to recall the order of events. He would get stuck on certain images or sounds, unable to move past them. As time went by, Asher became increasingly withdrawn. He stopped attending social gatherings, citing exhaustion or work commitments as excuses. He began to feel isolated and disconnected from those around him, as if there was an invisible wall between himself and others. He couldn't shake off the feeling that he was somehow responsible for what had happened - that if only he had acted faster or differently, things might have turned out better. Asher's relationships with his loved ones suffered. His wife noticed a change in him but couldn't pinpoint what it was. Asher felt like he was walking around with a perpetual sense of dread, always waiting for the other shoe to drop. He began to question his own ability to keep himself and those he cared about safe. At work, Asher's behavior became more erratic. He would snap at colleagues or overreact to minor setbacks. His designs became increasingly rigid and inflexible - as if he was trying to exert control over a chaotic world through the precision of lines and angles. It wasn't until his wife confronted him about the change in their relationship that Asher realized he needed help. She had noticed how jumpy he was, how easily startled by sudden noises or movements. Asher knew it was time to face what had been haunting him for so long - but he was terrified of confronting those memories and emotions head-on. As he sat in the therapist's office, Asher felt a sense of trepidation wash over him. He wasn't sure what lay ahead, but he knew he couldn't continue living like this - constantly on edge, always looking over his shoulder. For the first time in three years, Asher allowed himself to hope that maybe, just maybe, things could get better.
